quals-wisconsin-algebra-1994f-01.title: Normal p-complement arguments
quals-wisconsin-algebra-1994f-01.body:
**(i)** $|N|=|G|/|P|$ is prime to $p$, so by Lagrange every element of $N$ has order prime to $p$, and $N\cap P=1$. Then $|NP|=|N||P|=|G|$, so $G=NP$ and $G/N\cong P/(P\cap N)\cong P$ is a $p$-group. If $g\in G$ has order prime to $p$, its image in $G/N$ has order dividing both $o(g)$ and a power of $p$, so it is trivial: $g\in N$. Hence $N=\{g\in G: p
mid o(g)\}$.

**(ii)** Let $q
e p$ be a prime and $Q$ a Sylow $q$-subgroup of $N_G(P)$. By (i), $Q\subseteq N$. For $x\in Q$, $y\in P$: $[x,y]=x^{-1}(y^{-1}xy)\in N$ because $x\in N	rianglelefteq G$, and $[x,y]=(x^{-1}y^{-1}x)y\in P$ because $x$ normalizes $P$. So $[Q,P]\subseteq N\cap P=1$ and $Q$ centralizes $P$.

If $Q
e1$, pick $x\in Q$ of order $q$ and $y\in P$ of order $p$ (possible as $P
e1$). They commute, so $xy$ has order $pq$; it is not of $p$-power order, so by hypothesis $xy\in N$. But then by (i) its order is prime to $p$ — a contradiction. So every Sylow $q$-subgroup of $N_G(P)$ ($q
e p$) is trivial, i.e. $N_G(P)$ is a $p$-group containing the Sylow $p$-subgroup $P$. Hence $N_G(P)=P$. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-1994f-02.title: Use that R \ P is multiplicative
quals-wisconsin-algebra-1994f-02.body:
(We assume $1\in R$, acting as the identity on $V$.) Since $P$ is prime, $S=R\setminus P$ is closed under multiplication and contains $1$.

**(i)** $0\in W$ since $0\cdot1=0$. If $v_1a_1=0=v_2a_2$ with $a_i\in S$, then $(v_1+v_2)a_1a_2=0$ and $a_1a_2\in S$, so $v_1+v_2\in W$. For $r\in R$, $(v_1r)a_1=(v_1a_1)r=0$ (commutativity), so $v_1r\in W$. Thus $W$ is a submodule.

**(ii)** A finitely generated module over a Noetherian ring is Noetherian, so $W=w_1R+\dots+w_nR$. Pick $b_i\in S$ with $w_ib_i=0$ and put $b=b_1\cdots b_n\in S$. Then $w_ib=0$ for all $i$, so $Wb=\sum_i (w_iR)b=\sum_i (w_ib)R=0$.

**(iii)** Fix $0\ne v\in V$. Since $V$ is simple, $r\mapsto vr$ is a surjection $R\to V$ with kernel $M=\mathrm{ann}(v)$, and $R/M\cong V$ simple means $M$ is a maximal ideal. Since $W=0$, $v\notin W$, so no element of $S$ kills $v$: $M\cap S=\emptyset$, i.e. $M\subseteq P$. As $M$ is maximal and $P$ is proper, $P=M$ is maximal. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-1994f-03.title: Galois group of x^3 - 2
quals-wisconsin-algebra-1994f-03.body:
**(i)** Let $\theta=\sqrt[3]2$ and $\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}$. Then $E=\mathbb Q(\theta,\omega)=F(\omega)$, $|F:\mathbb Q|=3$ ($x^3-2$ is Eisenstein) and $|E:F|=2$ ($\omega\notin\mathbb R$), so $|G|=6$ and $G\cong\mathrm{Sym}_3$ acting on the roots $\theta,\omega\theta,\omega^2\theta$. Let $\sigma\in G$ with $\sigma(\theta)=\omega\theta$, $\sigma(\omega)=\omega$ (it exists: $E=\mathbb Q(\omega)(\theta)$ and $x^3-2$ is irreducible over $\mathbb Q(\omega)$ by degrees). Its fixed field $L$ satisfies $|E:L|=3$, so $|L:\mathbb Q|=2$ (in fact $L=\mathbb Q(\omega)$). Then $|F\cap L:\mathbb Q|$ divides $3$ and $2$, so $F\cap L=\mathbb Q$: the only elements of $F$ fixed by $\sigma$ are rational.

**(ii)** Let $a\in F$ with $a^3=c\in\mathbb Q$. If $a=0$ we are done. Otherwise $\sigma(a)$ is a root of $x^3-c$, whose roots are $a,\omega a,\omega^2a$; so $\sigma(a)=\omega^{-i}a$ for some $i\in\{0,1,2\}$. Then
$$\sigma(a\theta^i)=\omega^{-i}a\cdot\omega^i\theta^i=a\theta^i,$$
and $a\theta^i\in F$, so by (i) $a\theta^i\in\mathbb Q$. That is, one of $a$, $a\sqrt[3]2$, $a\sqrt[3]4$ is rational.

**(iii)** If $a=\sqrt[3]3\in E$, then $a\in E\cap\mathbb R=F$ and $a^3=3\in\mathbb Q$. By (ii), one of $\sqrt[3]3$, $\sqrt[3]6$, $\sqrt[3]{12}$ is rational. But $x^3-3$, $x^3-6$, $x^3-12$ are irreducible over $\mathbb Q$ by Eisenstein at $3$ (for $12$: $3\mid12$, $9\nmid12$), so none of these cube roots is rational. Hence $\sqrt[3]3\notin E$. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-1994f-04.title: Diagonalize over the algebraic closure
quals-wisconsin-algebra-1994f-04.body:
Work in $M_n(\bar K)\supseteq M_n(K)$. Since the characteristic polynomial has $n$ distinct roots $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n$, $A$ is diagonalizable over $\bar K$: $P^{-1}AP=D=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)$ with $P\in GL_n(\bar K)$.

If $Z=[z_{ij}]$ commutes with $D$, compare $(i,j)$ entries: $(ZD)_{ij}=z_{ij}\lambda_j$ and $(DZ)_{ij}=\lambda_iz_{ij}$, so $z_{ij}(\lambda_i-\lambda_j)=0$ and $z_{ij}=0$ for $i\ne j$. So the centralizer of $D$ consists of diagonal matrices.

Let $X,Y\in M_n(K)$ commute with $A$. Then $P^{-1}XP$ and $P^{-1}YP$ commute with $D$, hence are diagonal, hence commute with each other; conjugating back, $XY=YX$. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-1994f-05.title: Trace and simplicity of matrix rings
quals-wisconsin-algebra-1994f-05.body:
**(i)** If $s^k=0$ and $\lambda\in ar F$ is an eigenvalue of $s$ with eigenvector $v$, then $0=s^kv=\lambda^kv$, so $\lambda=0$. Thus the characteristic polynomial is $x^n$, and $\mathrm{tr}\,s$ (minus the $x^{n-1}$ coefficient, i.e. the sum of the eigenvalues with multiplicity) is $0$.

**(ii)** Since $	heta$ is surjective, $	heta(I)$ is a two-sided ideal of $S$: $	heta(r)	heta(i)=	heta(ri)\in	heta(I)$, and every element of $S$ is some $	heta(r)$. Every $x\in I$ is a sum of nilpotents $y_k$, and each $	heta(y_k)$ is nilpotent, so $\mathrm{tr}\,	heta(x)=\sum_k\mathrm{tr}\,	heta(y_k)=0$ by (i). In particular the matrix unit $e_{11}$, of trace $1$, is not in $	heta(I)$, so $	heta(I)
e S$. But $M_n(F)$ is a simple ring (any nonzero ideal contains some $a
e0$, and $e_{ii}=a_{kl}^{-1}e_{ik}ae_{li}$ for an entry $a_{kl}
e0$, so it contains $\sum e_{ii}=1$). Hence $	heta(I)=0$. ∎
